q: why do some birds migrate thousands of miles
why do species of birds migrate
migratory birds why do they migrate
a: Birds migrate primarily to find abundant food and suitable breeding conditions. The main drivers are seasonal changes that affect food availability: in temperate and arctic regions, insects, fruits, and seeds become scarce during winter, so insect-eating and fruit-eating birds must move to warmer areas where food remains available. Many birds also migrate to specific breeding grounds that offer abundant food for raising chicks during spring and summer, then return to wintering grounds. The Arctic Tern holds the record for the longest migration, traveling up to 44,000 miles (71,000 km) each year between the Arctic and Antarctic. Birds navigate using multiple cues: the sun's position during the day, the stars at night, the Earth's magnetic field (detected through specialized magnetoreceptors in their beaks or eyes), polarized light patterns, and even infrasound and landmarks. Some species learn migration routes from older birds, while others are genetically programmed with the route. Climate change is affecting migration patterns, causing some species to migrate earlier or shift their ranges northward. Not all birds migrate - resident birds have adapted to survive winter in place through behavioral and physiological adaptations.
